title: Yash Declares Cinema Has No Owners at Toxic Trailer Launch
excerpt: The KGF star used the Bengaluru launch of his upcoming film Toxic to call for a unified Indian cinema free of regional labels, in remarks seen as a response to producer Allu Aravind's earlier comments.
body:
• Kannada superstar Yash declared "Indian cinema isn't one person's property" at the trailer launch of his upcoming gangster drama Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown Ups in Bengaluru.
  • Yash said the industry should stop labeling films by language, calling Toxic "an Indian film" rather than a Kannada film.
  • The remarks are widely seen as an indirect response to Telugu producer Allu Aravind, who sparked controversy in 2023 by asking "Who was Yash before KGF?"
  • Toxic, directed by Geetu Mohandas, brings together cast and crew from multiple Indian film industries in a deliberate pan-Indian collaboration.

Kannada superstar Yash, the actor who became a nationwide phenomenon through the KGF franchise, used the trailer launch of his next film Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown Ups to make a pointed declaration about the future of Indian cinema.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZJSjdSECbjU

"From now on, this is not Kannada, Tamil, Telugu… This is an Indian film," Yash told the audience at the Bengaluru launch event. "Indian cinema isn't one person's property."

A Response Without Naming Names

Yash never mentioned producer Allu Aravind by name, but the context was impossible to miss. In November 2023, the Telugu producer — father of superstar Allu Arjun — triggered a social media firestorm when he asked, "Who was Yash before KGF?" during a public discussion about actors' fees and film budgets.

https://x.com/ASKEnterta33271/status/2088940710565400994

Aravind's point was that big-budget filmmaking, not star power alone, drives box office success. "The lead actor of a movie gets only 20 to 25 percent of the film's budget as remuneration," he said at the time. "It is because of the making that it attracts the audience." But the phrasing stung. Yash's fans flooded social media with furious responses, some pointing out that Allu Arjun himself was a "tier-2" actor before his breakout with Ala Vaikunthapurramuloo.

"Who was Yash before the release of the KGF movie? Why did that movie make noise? It was that richness that led to the success of the movie."

— Allu Aravind, producer, November 2023

Sources close to both camps later said Aravind had clarified his remarks with Yash directly, and Yash reportedly took no personal offense. When Allu Arjun publicly praised Yash after KGF: Chapter 2, Yash responded warmly, calling him "awesome" and saying he had "always admired" him.

Toxic as a Pan-Indian Statement

With Toxic, Yash appears to be making a statement through his work rather than words. The film, directed by acclaimed Kerala-born filmmaker Geetu Mohandas, deliberately assembles talent from multiple Indian film industries — a casting and crew strategy that embodies the borderless cinema Yash advocates.

"Every actor is selfish. That's a fact," Yash said at the event, before clarifying he meant it constructively — every performer naturally wants to deliver their best work. But for Toxic, he said, everyone set aside personal egos. Actors and technicians who had already earned reputations in their own industries collaborated with one shared goal: the film's success.

The gangster drama is generating significant anticipation, and its trailer has drawn a strong response. Yash positioned it not as his film but as a collective effort — a distinction that carries weight in an industry where star hierarchies and regional loyalties have traditionally defined production and distribution.

The Bigger Picture

Yash's call for a unified Indian cinema arrives at a moment when the lines between regional film industries are blurring faster than ever. The KGF franchise itself — a Kannada-language production that grossed over ₹1,200 crore worldwide — proved that a film from any language can capture a national audience. Pushpa, RRR, and Kantara reinforced the same point from Telugu and Kannada cinema.

For the Indian diaspora, which often consumes films across languages without the regional loyalties that shape domestic markets, this shift toward pan-Indian storytelling resonates. The question is no longer which language a film is made in, but whether it connects — a philosophy Yash seems determined to push forward with Toxic.
nri_angle: Yash's advocacy for a borderless Indian cinema resonates with the diaspora audience, which watches films across languages and cares more about storytelling quality than regional labels.
author: Diaspora Desk
